Upon hatching, the veliger larvae undergo a brief free-swimming phase before settling onto submerged vegetation, where they begin grazing on periphyton and detritus. As juveniles continue to develop, they progress through a series of instars characterized by gradual increases in shell dimensions. Sexual maturation is typically attained once the shell reaches a height of 0.4 centimeters [Lp = 0.4 centimeters], at which point the gonads become fully functional and gametogenesis commences. The onset of reproductive activity is further accelerated in warmer waters, where metabolic rates are elevated and growth proceeds more rapidly. Comparative studies with other planorbid snails suggest that a relatively small size at maturity is an adaptation to unpredictable hydrologic environments, where early reproduction enhances the probability of contributing offspring before habitat desiccation occurs. Consequently, Bulinus tropicus invests heavily in early fecundity at the expense of maximum somatic size.

This asymptotic dimension is seldom reached in natural populations, where resource limitation and periodic desiccation events truncate growth before individuals can achieve their full potential. In stable laboratory aquaria with ad libitum food supplies, however, a small proportion of individuals do approach this upper boundary, exhibiting a characteristic deceleration in growth rate as they approach their terminal size. The species' small adult stature likely confers several ecological advantages, including reduced absolute metabolic demands and the ability to exploit thin water films and marginal microhabitats unavailable to larger congeners. Additionally, the compact shell morphology facilitates rapid population turnover, enabling Bulinus tropicus to rebound quickly from environmental perturbations. This combination of small ultimate size and high fecundity exemplifies a ruderal life-history strategy common among pioneering species of disturbed or ephemeral freshwater systems.

Field mark-recapture studies have corroborated these laboratory findings, with snails collected during the cool winter months exhibiting higher survivorship probabilities than those active during the summer breeding season. Nevertheless, this potential longevity provides a useful demographic parameter for constructing population models of this species.

The reproductive biology of Bulinus tropicus is characterized by a capacity for continuous, rapid egg production when environmental conditions remain favorable. Adult females are capable of depositing egg masses containing multiple embryos several times per week, contributing to the species' high intrinsic rate of increase. The maximum rate of egg output recorded in this species is equivalent to 20 eggs per 7 days [Ri = 20 eggs per 7 days], a figure that was documented in a controlled laboratory experiment where snails were provided with abundant food and maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This elevated temperature substantially boosts metabolic and reproductive activity, though it simultaneously shortens individual lifespan relative to cooler conditions. The trade-off between high fecundity at elevated temperatures and reduced longevity at those same temperatures is a central theme in the life-history ecology of this snail, reflecting a classic fast-slow continuum within a single species. Continued observation of this species across its thermal range will further elucidate the physiological mechanisms underlying these plastic responses.
